## **Building the Metric Graph**

In this section, we construct the metric graph for the road network. The graph is the foundation for all subsequent analyses.

Let us start by setting some global options for all code.
```{r  setup, include=FALSE}
# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(42) 
# Set global options for all code chunks
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  # Disable messages printed by R code chunks
  message = FALSE,    
  # Disable warnings printed by R code chunks
  warning = FALSE,    
  # Show R code within code chunks in output
  echo = TRUE,        
  # Include both R code and its results in output
  include = TRUE,     
  # Evaluate R code chunks
  eval = TRUE,       
  # Enable caching of R code chunks for faster rendering
  cache = FALSE,      
  # Align figures in the center of the output
  fig.align = "center",
  # Enable retina display for high-resolution figures
  retina = 2,
  # Show errors in the output instead of stopping rendering
  error = TRUE,
  # Do not collapse code and output into a single block
  collapse = FALSE
)
```

Load the necessary libraries.

```{r}
# Load libraries
library(MetricGraph)
library(ggplot2)
library(sp)
library(sf)
library(mapview)
library(dplyr)
library(qs)
library(tidyr)
library(leaflet)
library(DataExplorer)

library(here)
library(rmarkdown)
library(grateful) # Cite all loaded packages
```

Here we start with prepared data from TomTom, a commercial traffic data provider. The data includes road segments with attributes such as length, speed limit, and traffic intensity. We will filter and transform this data to create a graph for the city center of Ahsa.
The `FRC' stands for the Functional Road Class, which is a classification of roads based on their importance and function. The FRC ranges from 1 to 7, with 1 being the highest class (e.g., highways) and 7 the lowest class (e.g., local roads). We start by checking the data structure and missing values.

```{r}
# Load data
load(here("Data/tomtom_ahsa_extended.RData"))
tomtom <- data
rm(data)

# Convert FRC to numeric and plot missing values
tomtom$FRC <- as.numeric(tomtom$FRC)
plot_missing(tomtom)

hist(tomtom$SpeedLimit)
unique(tomtom$SpeedLimit)
```

The full data derived from the TomTom contains 256,745 road segments, and covers spatially all accidents in the dataset. We will filter the data to include only the road segments within the city center of Ahsa, to reduce the computational load. The map of the whole data is shown below colored according to road class.

```{r, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cat('<iframe src="road_class_map.html" width="100%" height="600px" style="border:none;"></iframe>')
```

The speed limit values are not rounded to the nearest 10, which is common in practice. We will round the speed limit values and compute the traffic intensity based on the speed limit, road length, and functional road class (FRC). The traffic intensity is a measure of traffic flow on a road segment, which we will use as a covariate in the LGCP model.

```{r}
# Round to the nearest tenth
tomtom$SpeedLimit <- round(tomtom$SpeedLimit / 10) * 10
hist(tomtom$SpeedLimit)
unique(tomtom$SpeedLimit)

# Join FRC 0 and 1 classes
tomtom$FRC[tomtom$FRC == 0] <- 1 
hist(tomtom$FRC)
```

```{r}
# Load polygon boundary for the city center
polygon <- st_read(here("Data/center_ahsa_polygon.geojson")) %>%
  st_cast("POLYGON") %>%
  st_transform(crs = st_crs(tomtom))

# Visualize the polygon boundary
leaflet() %>%
  addProviderTiles("CartoDB.Positron") %>%
  addPolygons(data = polygon, color = "red", fill = FALSE, weight = 2)
```


```{r}
# Filter and transform TomTom data for the city center
filter_transform_tomtom <- function(data, polygon) {
  data %>%
    dplyr::select(Segment.Id, Length, FRC, SpeedLimit, geometry) %>%
    mutate(Length_km = Length / 1000) %>%
    st_transform(crs = st_crs(data)) %>%
    st_filter(x = ., y = polygon, .predicate = st_within)
}

tomtom_sub <- filter_transform_tomtom(tomtom, polygon)

# Inspect the filtered data
str(tomtom_sub) # [178,807 × 6] graph with FRC7
```

We recommend to use the high-precision data, when available, to construct large-scale graphs. This will ensure fast and accurate graph construction. Given such high-precision, one can safely put the `merge_close_vertices` argument in the `graph_components$new()` to `FALSE`. This will prevent the merging of close vertices, and therefore speed up significantly the graph construction and also reduce computational memory load. You can view all the steps of the graph construction by setting the `verbose` argument to 1 or 2 (more detailed).

```{r, eval=FALSE, include=T}
# New way to directly build the graph
system.time({
  graph = graph_components$new(edges = tomtom_sub,  merge_close_vertices = FALSE, verbose=1)
})
 # user  system elapsed 
 # 50.764   0.290  51.297

graph$n

# Get the largest connected component
graph_ahsa <- graph$get_largest()

# Save the graph object with high compression
qsave(graph_ahsa, "Data/graph_weighted_7FRC_city_center.qs", preset = "high")

```

We further prune the graph, i.e. remove the vertices with degree 2 without changing the graph structure. This will reduce the number of vertices and edges, and speed up the computation of the LGCP model. Note that, here we add the edge weights to the graph object, because we will use them as spatial covariates in the LGCP model. This will ensure the dimensional compatibility between the graph and the covariates. Since edge weights are added beforehand, pruning will involve comparison of the weights on edges, and ensure we are only removing vertices with degree 2 that have the same edge weights. For practical purposes, this means that we are checking if the road is of the same type and has the same speed limit, and only then we remove the vertices. 


```{r, eval=FALSE, include=T}
graph <- qread("Data/graph_weighted_7FRC_city_center.qs")
graph$set_edge_weights(weights = graph$get_edge_weights() %>% select(FRC, SpeedLimit))
graph$get_edge_weights()
system.time({
  graph$prune_vertices(verbose=2)
})
#  user  system elapsed 
# 544.501  41.383 588.785 

# Save the graph object with high compression
qsave(graph, "Data/graph_weighted_7FRC_city_center_pruned.qs", preset = "high")
```

The summary of the pruned graph is shown below. The graph has 67223 vertices and 164586 edges. 
```{r}
graph <- qread(here("Data/graph_weighted_7FRC_city_center_pruned.qs"))
summary(graph)
```
The graph is visualized using the `mapview` package.
```{r}
graph$plot(vertex_size = 0, type = "mapview", edge_width = 0.05,edge_color = "blue")
```

## **Build mesh for LGCP fitting**

After constructing the graph, we need to set up the mesh for the LGCP model. 
Even though we do not use the finite element method (FEM) for approximating the the Whittle--Matérn field $u(s)$, we still need to set up the mesh for LGCP model.

The mesh is built with a resolution of 50 meters, and we also build a coarser mesh with a resolution of 100 meters for sensitivity analysis. The parameter `h` in the `build_mesh()` function controls the mesh resolution. The value of `h` is in the same units as the graph, which is in kilometers. Therefore, `h = 0.05` corresponds to a mesh resolution of 50 meters.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Load graph and build mesh
setup_graph_mesh <- function() {
  graph <- qread("Data/graph_weighted_7FRC_city_center_pruned.qs")
  graph$build_mesh(h=0.05)
  qsave(graph, "Data/graph_mesh_pruned_50m_7FRC.qs")
  }
system.time({
  setup_graph_mesh()
})
 #  user  system elapsed 
 # 54.089  11.074  65.385 
```

The graph is now ready for the LGCP model fitting. The additional step is to prepare the spatial covariates for the LGCP model. We will cover this in the next section. If you are interested in the LGCP model fitting without covariates, please refer to the [Model 1](model1.html) page.

### Mesh sensitivity

The mesh resolution is an important factor in the LGCP model fitting. It is worth clarifying what the mesh is used for. Recall that the log-likelihood of the LGCP model involves two components: (i) the integral $\int_\Gamma \lambda(s) \, ds$, which is approximated numerically using a mid-point rule with integration weights $\tilde{a}_i$ at mesh nodes, and (ii) the evaluation of the intensity $\lambda(s_i)$ at each observed point location. The Whittle--Matérn field $u(s)$ is evaluated **exactly** at all locations (both mesh nodes and observation points) via its Markov properties --- no finite element approximation of the field is needed. Therefore, the mesh controls the accuracy of the numerical integration only, not the approximation of the Gaussian field itself. The spatial covariates, however, must also be available at each mesh node, so the mesh resolution also determines at what spatial resolution the covariates enter the model.

The mesh resolution can be adjusted by changing the `h` parameter in the `build_mesh()` function. The value of `h` is in the same units as the graph coordinates. In our case, the graph units are in kilometers, so `h = 0.05` corresponds to a mesh resolution of 50 meters.

To assess the sensitivity of the posterior results to the choice of mesh, we conducted a simulation study on the application graph. We simulated log-Gaussian Cox processes with an intercept and one covariate under two parameter settings: (i) $\kappa = \tau = 0.5$, and (ii) $\kappa = 0.33, \tau = 0.61$. The latent field was generated on a fine 10 m mesh, treated as ground truth. For each setting, we generated multiple replicates and estimated the model using meshes with resolutions $h \in \{200, 100, 50, 25\}$ meters.

```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Mesh sensitivity analysis for LGCP parameter recovery. Posterior mean estimates ($\\pm$95% CI) of the SPDE parameters κ and τ for mesh resolutions from 200 m to 25 m. Dashed lines indicate true simulation values. Top row: κ = τ = 0.5. Bottom row: κ = 0.33, τ = 0.61. Parameter estimates converge toward true values as mesh resolution increases, with h = 50 m achieving acceptable accuracy."}
knitr::include_graphics("Figures/mesh_sensitivity_combined_clean.png")
```

At coarse resolutions ($h = 200$ m), parameter estimates exhibit substantial bias (approximately 50--70% relative error in $\kappa$). At $h = 100$ m, estimates approach the true values with relative errors of approximately 10--15%. At $h = 50$ m, recovery is near-perfect (< 5% relative error). Based on these findings, we adopt $h = 50$ m for the application as it provides adequate accuracy while remaining computationally tractable. That said, $h = 100$ m is still a reasonable choice for this graph if computational resources are limited.
